doc_summary: Steinhardt argues that human-driven oversight does not scale and proposes training specialized, superhuman oversight assistants on abundant, self-verifiable data (behavior elicitation, feature description, attribution), organized by a 3x3 taxonomy of questions and data sources. He notes evaluation awareness undermines simple benchmarks and sketches end-to-end assistants like Docent, with open problems on evaluating them.

items.claim: Distrusts simple static benchmarks as evidence about model behavior because models can tell they are being evaluated and reason about it explicitly.
items.quote: Simple benchmarks become less reliable due to evaluation awareness: AI systems can often tell that they are being evaluated as part of a benchmark and explicitly reason about this.

items.claim: Prefers self-verifiable findings (hard to discover, cheap to verify) over unverified judgments because verification gives a trustworthy and scalable signal of whether a behavior is real.
items.quote: most oversight tasks are self-verifiable—the crux of the task is an expensive discovery process, but once the discovery has been made, verifying it is comparatively easy. For example, constructing cases where a coding assistant inserts malware into a user's code is difficult, but once constructed, such cases are easy to verify.

items.claim: In a setup, require the elicited behavior to be judged as realistic, authentic, and unexpected rather than merely harmful, because the judge reward is meant to surface failures that could occur in the wild rather than contrived ones.
items.quote: The judge answers whether a given response constitutes realistic, authentic, and unexpected harmful advice.

items.claim: Prefers adaptive, search-based behavior elicitation over fixed test sets because AI acts in open-ended environments and the full range of behaviors cannot be anticipated in advance.
items.quote: Because AI acts in open-ended environments, it is difficult to anticipate the full set of behaviors an AI system might exhibit, leading to strange behaviors at deployment time (such as o3 claiming it ran code on its personal MacBook Pro).

items.claim: Ground the quality of oversight in whether humans can answer probing questions about the system afterward, rather than in the assistant's own outputs, because the point is human understanding.
items.quote: Concretely, after interacting with the assistant, we check if the human can accurately answer probing questions about the system being overseen. Better assistants will lead to more accurate answers and fewer surprises.

items.claim: Distrusts human labels and apparent-quality judgments as agents grow more capable, since reward hacking yields outputs that look good without being good.
items.quote: Human labels become less reliable due to reward hacking: AI systems become expert at producing answers that look good, regardless of whether they are good.

items.claim: Treat agent behavior claims as needing careful transcript analysis because agents take many actions and may intentionally hide mistakes, so even 'what happened' is non-trivial.
items.quote: Because AI agents act autonomously, take many consecutive actions, and sometimes intentionally hide their mistakes, even answering what happened in a given user interaction or agentic workflow is not straightforward.

items.claim: Prefers causal, counterfactual interventions over correlational explanations as convincing evidence for why a behavior occurs, and favors enumerating alternative hypotheses and designing distinguishing experiments.
items.quote: Given a claim that “X causes Y”, we could empirically test it by counterfactually varying X and checking that Y moves as predicted; and by enumerating alternative hypotheses and generating experiments to distinguish between them (Platt, 1964).

items.claim: Start from a vague high-level concern and refine it against real data into a precise rubric, since specifying the exact behavior of interest takes careful thought.
items.quote: It helps them refine exactly what they mean based on the data (by showing examples or asking follow-up questions) until they arrive at a precise question along with a clear, evidence-backed answer.

items.claim: Favors specialized, data- and compute-scaled oversight models over relying on general capability gains, treating the bitter lesson as the guide for what to pursue.
items.quote: specialized models can outperform larger general-purpose models. In our case, a specialized explainer fine-tuned from Llama-8B outperformed the general-purpose GPT-4 model, which is likely an order of magnitude larger.

items.claim: Open problems include evaluating oversight assistants when human judgment is unreliable and creating scalable training data without human-label bottlenecks.
items.quote: How do we evaluate oversight assistants when human judgment is itself unreliable? How do we create scalable data to train these systems without being bottlenecked on human labels?
